Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette:
Bao presents as a 35-year-old UX designer, married, who has been struggling since a significant health crisis eight months prior. The event occurred on what felt like a perfectly ordinary Tuesday. He was at his office, leading a design sprint for a new mobile app, when a crushing pressure bloomed in his chest. At first, he dismissed it as indigestion or stress, trying to push through the meeting. He remembers the minutes stretching into an eternity as he tried to focus on the wireframes while a cold sweat slicked his skin. The delay in acknowledging the severity of his symptoms became a central, terrifying feature of the memory. By the time he finally collapsed and a colleague called 911, he was certain he was dying. The chaotic ambulance ride and the frantic efficiency of the emergency room are now a blur of disconnected sounds and flashes of light, a memory fragment he actively works to suppress.

In the months since his recovery from what doctors termed a 'major cardiac event,' Bao’s world has progressively shrunk. His body feels constantly tense, a coiled spring perpetually ready to react to a danger only he can perceive. This hypervigilance is most acute at his job. When a webpage takes an extra second to load or a colleague is two minutes late for a virtual meeting, his mind immediately leaps to catastrophic conclusions—a system-wide crash is imminent, his colleague has been in a terrible accident. He understands, on a rational level, that these are improbable, but the physical sensation of panic is overwhelming. He cannot trust assurances of safety, even from his own wife, Lien, or his cardiologist. When they tell him he is healthy and the danger has passed, the words feel hollow. The only truth he can access is the relentless tension in his shoulders and the shallow, watchful quality of his own breath.

To manage this pervasive sense of threat, Bao has constructed a life defined by avoidance. He has mapped out a new, longer route to work to circumvent the hospital district, the sight of the building alone enough to make his heart hammer in his chest. He deleted the health app from his phone and has cancelled two consecutive follow-up physicals, unable to bear the thought of a doctor listening to his chest. Any situation that puts his body under stress is now unthinkable. He was once an avid cyclist, but now he avoids even a brisk walk, terrified that a rising heart rate will trigger another event. When thoughts of that day in the office surface, he immediately immerses himself in the most complex coding problem he can find, forcing the memories out with lines of intricate logic.

These strategies have come at a cost. Bao has come to believe there is something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, that his body and his mind are both defective. He sees his colleagues moving through their lives with an ease he can no longer imagine and is convinced that his inability to "move on" is a sign of profound personal weakness. This belief is compounded by a pervasive emotional numbness. He describes feeling "dead inside," as if he is watching his own life from behind a thick pane of glass. He sits beside Lien on the sofa in the evenings, aware that he should feel love or comfort, but feels only a vast, grey emptiness. It was this hollowness, and Lien’s tearful confession that she felt she was "living with a ghost," that finally prompted him to seek help. He is now terrified of revisiting the trauma in therapy, yet more terrified of continuing to live a life devoid of feeling, forever on alert for a danger that has already passed.
